title: The Merging of Difference and Unity
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the Sandokai, "The Merging of Difference and Unity," the poem by the eighth-century Chinese master Shitou that the sangha has just chanted. Seishu explains the title's three characters, including the merchants who break a wooden board in half and rejoin it to confirm an agreement, and ties the poem to the Heart Sutra's "form is emptiness" and to a passage from Karen Armstrong's book on the Buddha. Four sections of the poem follow, with the body as an orchestra and light and dark as the front and back foot in walking. Seishu then tells of a sleepless night when an ordinary cup of tea tasted like the best of Seishu's life, and closes with Dogen's instructions to the cook.

Well, I would also like to welcome all of you and thank you for coming in this age of separation.
It's really nice to be able to see people even electronically.
It feels like much more of a connection than if we were just on the phone.
I'm very grateful for the technology that allows us to meet in this way.
So thanks again for being here.
I'm going to talk about the poem that we just chanted, The Merging of Difference and Unity.
It was written in the 8th century by the Chinese Zen master Shitou.
He lived in southern China from 700 to 790, so he had a very long life.
He's known mainly for this piece of writing and one of the most important other poem.
Then we have a few dialogues between him and some of his students, but otherwise we know very little about him.
We do know one thing though, and that is that he emphasized sitting meditation, zazen, as an essential part of practice.
The reason that we know that is that in the 13th century, the Japanese priest Eihei Dogen wrote about him.
As many of you know, Dogen is considered the founder of Soto Zen.
So here's what Dogen says about Shitou.
*Great master Shitou did zazen on a large rock where he had a thatched hut.
He sat continuously without sleeping day or night, although he did not ignore work.
He did not fail to do zazen throughout the day.*

I think this means that Shitou did not need to be sitting on a cushion to pay full attention to every breath and every moment of his life, whether he was working, meditating, or meeting with students.
He paid full attention to every moment of his life.
The title of this poem, The Merging of Difference and Unity, in Japanese is called Sandokai, and it has three parts to it.
San means difference, diversity, or variety.
These are the unique things in life: objects, people, the phenomenal aspects of life.
The second character, Dou, means sameness or equality.
It's a synonym for the absolute ultimate reality of life, beyond discrimination.
Everything is connected: unity.
The last character, Kai, means promise or agreement.
In ancient China, when two merchants made an agreement, they would write it on a wooden board and then break the board in half, with each merchant taking one half.
Later, when they exchanged goods, they would put the pieces of the board together to make sure that the agreement had been met.
So Sandokai refers to the agreement between these two aspects of life: the concrete, composed of objects, evaluations, ideas, and the absolute side of life, where everything is connected.
Nothing is separate.
Both sides of life exist and they work together.
The translation for Sandokai that we use is the merging of difference and unity.
The theme of separateness and unity appears quite often in Buddhist writing.
In the Heart Sutra, which we frequently chant here, the terms are a little bit different, but they mean the same thing.

There's a line in the Heart Sutra that says, *form is emptiness and emptiness is form.* Form means objects, separate objects like san, and emptiness means that things are empty of separation, so they are connected, which is similar to do.
Emptiness is a hard term to understand, but one way to understand it and describe it is to say that nothing exists independently.
Nothing is unchanging and exists all by itself.
Everything depends on everything else.
For example, my life depends on my parents and their parents and their parents.
Go back as far as you want.
It depends on oxygen in the air.
It depends on farmers growing food, which depends on the sun and the rain and the soil and people to take food to the grocery store.
Without all these things, I wouldn't exist and neither would any of us.
Everything depends on other things for existence.
Everything supports everything else.
That's one way to describe emptiness.
The Heart Sutra says that form is included in emptiness and emptiness is included in form.
This is like two sides of a coin.
One side looks different from the other side, but they're connected.
Here's one more example of this connection between the relative and the absolute, or between the sacred and the ordinary.
This is a quote from Karen Armstrong's book, Buddha.
The book is a biography of the Buddha, but it has quite a bit about the Buddha's teachings in it.
So this is something from Karen Armstrong's book.
*The attainment of Nirvana did not mean that the Buddha would never experience any more suffering.
He would grow old, get sick and die like everybody else, and he would experience pain while doing so.

Nirvana does not give an awakened person trance like immunity from suffering, but an inner haven which enables a man or a woman to live with pain to take possession of it, affirm it, and experience a profound peace of mind in the midst of suffering.
Nirvana, therefore, is found within oneself in the very heart of each person's being.
It's an entirely natural state.
It is not bestowed by grace nor achieved for us by a supernatural savior.
It can be reached by anybody who cultivates the path as assiduously as the Buddha did.
Nirvana is a still center.
It gives meaning to life.*
So Nirvana is not some condition or state of mind or place out there.
If it happens, it happens in the midst of our messy lives with all of their problems.
It could happen in a traffic jam.
It could happen in the midst of a painful physical or emotional situation, or it can happen in a beautiful setting out in nature.
This is what the merging of difference and unity is talking about.
Reality includes everything.
There's no separation between the sacred and the ordinary.
We don't have time today to go over every single line of the poem and explore its meaning.
I picked four different sections to talk about.
If you're interested in reading about the merging of difference and unity, a couple of good books on that would be Living by Vow by Shohaku Okumura.
He talks about this chant, plus many of the other chants that we chant: the Heart Sutra, the Enmei Jukku, things like that.
He's a very good writer.
Another good book on the merging of difference and unity is Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness by Shunryu Suzuki Roshi.
I'm going to start with the first lines of the poem.
*The mind of the great sage of India is intimately transmitted from west to east, while human faculties are sharp or dull, the way has no northern or southern ancestors.*
So the mind of the great sage of India is Buddha's mind, the mind that takes in everything, both ordinary life and sacred life, and can see all of it.
Buddhism came from India to China, so that's west to east.
Seeing things the way the Buddha saw things can be passed on from person to person.
In Zen, we use the expression "warm hand to warm hand."
It's an intimate practice.
It involves having a regular meditation practice, having a sangha, a group of people to practice with, and usually having a teacher.
Anyone and everyone is capable of awakening, regardless of gender, regardless of position in society or mental faculties.
In Shitou's time, there were several schools of Buddhism with different approaches and opinions about how to practice.
"The way has no northern or southern ancestors" means that Buddha's teaching includes both the northern and southern schools.
Even if you don't understand the teaching, it reaches everywhere, and arguing about the different schools is not productive.
So the next section I will talk about, I'll read it for you:
*All of the objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement, otherwise each keeps its place.*
This is about seeing life from both sides, independent and at the same time interconnected.
Only the eyes see, only the tongue tastes, only the ears hear.
If you lose your sight, your ears and your tongue won't replace the function of the eyes.
So in a sense they're all independent, and yet each one needs the whole body in order to function: heart, lungs, brain, blood vessels.
Nothing works by itself.
In writing about this, Shōhaku Okumura compares the body to an orchestra.
There are many different instruments, each playing a different part, and one instrument can't replace another.
The violin can't replace the clarinet.
So you have all these different musicians playing different sounds, but they combine to make one piece of music.
The next section I'll talk about is this one:
*In the light, there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.
In the dark, there is light, but don't see it as light.
Light and dark oppose one another, like the front and back foot in walking.*
Here light means the relative visible world that we live in.
Objects can be seen and distinctions can be made: big, little, I like it, I don't like it, good, bad.
Darkness refers to the absolute world that is beyond our words and our intellectual understanding.
There are no distinctions.
There's no separation.
Everything is merged in the pitch black.
You can't distinguish anything.
You can't even see your hand in front of your face.
Light and darkness are always together.
The mystery is present in the phenomenal world, so there's darkness in the light, and the phenomenal world exists within the mystery of life, so there's light in the darkness.
We have a much more limited life if we can only see life from one perspective, to only see independence or to only see interdependence.
There may be times when we need to give our full attention to the relative side of life and only see that side.
So that means don't see darkness in the light.
And if we have an experience of the absolute, we have to hold off on analyzing it or it'll be gone.
Just as we need both feet to walk and keep our balance, we need the perspective and the experience of both independence and interconnection to live our lives as fully and compassionately as we can.
So I want to say something about the world beyond our rational mind.
They say in Zen, I'm losing my voice here, they say in Zen that if you try to go after a certain experience, you won't get it.
Striving and grasping for something doesn't work.

With regular meditation, you practice learning to just be still and observe what is arising in the body and in the mind, what emotions are happening and what the senses are picking up around you, without adding anything: without adding likes and dislikes, without adding resistance or storylines.
This is the mind of Buddha.
It's vast like the sky.

It takes a lot of practice, because we are always getting pulled away from just paying attention to our lives by thoughts and feelings and memories and wishes for the future or regrets about the past, and we have to come back over and over and over again to the breath and the body, 10,000 times.
Once in a while, the absolute side of life might find you, and that would be life as it appears before the mind evaluates and labels our experience.
Some years ago, I was having trouble sleeping and I woke up in the middle of the night.
I knew that I wasn't going to be able to go back to sleep soon, so I thought, well, I'll just get up.
I went downstairs and left all the lights off and wandered around the kitchen for a while, and then I thought, well, I'll just have a cup of tea.
So I put the kettle on and got a cup and dropped a teabag in the cup, and when the water boiled I put the water in there and let it sit for a while.

Then I picked up the cup and started to walk into the living room, and I noticed, oh, the warmth of the cup felt really good, and I could see the steam rising from the cup, and I could smell the tea, and it just smelled terrific.
I sat down and took a sip and it tasted so good, and when I swallowed, I could feel it go all the way down my throat into my stomach.
I don't know how long that little experience lasted, but it was the best cup of tea I ever had in my life, and it was the same tea that I drink every day.
As soon as I started to go, oh my god, this is amazing, it was gone, just back to an average cup of tea.
But I thought that was a great example of a little bit of the sacred mixed in with ordinary life.
The last thing, then: I'll read the last section of the poem, and then we'll talk about it a little bit.
*If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.
I respectfully urge you who study the mystery: do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
We're always in the midst of reality, but we often lose sight of it with opinions and desires and stories that we've added.
We have to keep letting go of all the things that we've added.
And when we wake up to the way things are, and Suzuki Roshi would use this term, "things as it is," the way, the path, is right in front of us.
This is life without likes and dislikes, concepts or storylines, just being fully present.
And the path of practice is always right by our side, whether we know it or not.

We meditate regularly, we try to pay attention to our day-to-day lives, we try to respond skillfully to whatever situation we find ourselves in, whether it's at home, at work, as a parent, with friends.
Try to be kind, try to be patient.
When we make a mistake, hopefully we will notice it and think about it without being too harsh on ourselves, and then either try to make a correction or at least try not to repeat the mistake.
Just live day-to-day life right where you are, and don't look too far ahead.
What am I going to be like in a few years if I keep doing this?
What's my meditation going to be like?
Will I become awakened?
Of course we want our practice to do some good, but if you put too much emphasis on progress, that's a problem.
So make effort without too much desire about what the results will be.
Mountains and rivers are the internal barriers that we create ourselves.
I should be further along, other people are better at this than I am, I should be having different experiences in my meditation, that kind of thing.
It's important to be clear about practice: how to meditate, how to have an upright posture, how to pay attention and how to let go of all the things that interfere with that.
And it's important to use Buddhist teachings in day-to-day life.
Make a sincere, strong effort, but don't worry about near or far.
Do not use your days and nights in vain.
Our lives go on for a while and then they're over, so we don't have forever to practice.
What do you want to give your life energy to in the limited time that we all have?
Let me finish with another quote from Dogen, from his instructions to the cook.
*It is vital that we clarify and harmonize our lives with our work and not lose sight of either the absolute or the practical.*
So thank you for listening, and that's what I have to say about the merging of difference and unity.
I think now Chris is going to put us into small groups for a short discussion.
The way it works, I think, is you'll get invited to join a group, and when you get that invitation, hopefully you'll accept.

Then we'll have maybe ten minutes or so to just take turns making any comment you have about either the chant we did or the talk I gave or anything about the sacred and the ordinary in your day-to-day life, any of that kind of stuff.
I'll turn it back over to Chris to put us into small groups, and thank you again.
John, you were going to tell me how many small groups?
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight.
I think we could do, let's see, do we have, what do we have?
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
I think we have about eleven people, so what if we do four small groups?
Four small groups?
I can't hear you.
Four small groups?
Yeah.
Okay.
And so I'm going to pause the recording.
I'm actually going to stop it.
